title: Path Operations, Joining, Breaking & Stroke Joins
subtitle: Join Curves, Break, Close, Reverse, Miter Limits & Cap Profiles

learningObjectives: Execute fundamental path operations: Join Curves, Break Curve, Close Curve, and Reverse Curve.
Understand path winding direction and its impact on fills, Boolean operations, and Text-on-Path.
Master the Stroke Studio: Butt, Round, and Square Cap styles.
Configure corner Join styles: Miter Join (with threshold limits), Round Join, and Bevel Join.
Diagnose and eliminate stroke spikes caused by excessive miter limits on acute angles.
standardSections.foundationalKnowledge: In vector illustration, an open curve has distinct start and end endpoints, while a closed curve forms an unbroken perimeter loop. Often in complex drafting, multiple individual line segments must be merged into a single continuous vector outline (Join Curves), or a path must be uncoupled at a specific vertex (Break Curve). Furthermore, stroke geometry is not purely mathematical hairpins—it possesses physical thickness governed by Cap styles (how stroke ends terminate) and Join styles (how two line segments meet at an angle). Controlling the Miter Limit is vital to avoid unsightly giant spikes poking out from acute sharp angles.

technicalEvidence.source: Affinity Designer 3.3.3 Stroke Studio & Curve Operation Documentation

shortcut.win: View > Studio > Stroke (or Context Toolbar Actions)
shortcut.mac: View > Studio > Stroke (or Context Toolbar Actions)

toolAndFeatureExplanation.description: Path operation buttons reside on the Node Tool Context Toolbar (Join Curves, Break Curve, Close Curve, Reverse Curve). The Stroke Studio governs width, alignment, caps, joins, and miter limits.
contextBarOptions: Join Curves: Merges two separate selected curves into one continuous path
Break Curve: Splits a single curve at the selected node into two independent open endpoints
Close Curve: Automatically bridges start and end nodes with a closing segment
Reverse Curve: Inverts the internal directional sequence of nodes
Cap Options: Butt Cap (flat at node), Round Cap (semicircle), Square Cap (extends by half width)
Join Options: Miter Join (sharp), Round Join (curved), Bevel Join (clipped bevel)

stepByStepInstructions.title: Draw Two Disconnected Paths
stepByStepInstructions.instruction: Using the Pen Tool (P), draw two separate curved line segments side-by-side on your canvas. Notice they appear as two separate '(Curve)' layers in the Layers Studio.

stepByStepInstructions.title: Join Two Curves into One Continuous Path
stepByStepInstructions.instruction: Switch to the Node Tool (A). Hold Shift and select both curves. Marquee-select the two neighboring endpoints that you want to unite. On the Context Toolbar, click the 'Join Curves' button. The two endpoints weld together into a single continuous path!

stepByStepInstructions.title: Break a Path at a Specific Vertex
stepByStepInstructions.instruction: Select any anchor point along your continuous curve. On the Context Toolbar, click 'Break Curve'. The node splits into two open endpoints, allowing you to pull them apart.

stepByStepInstructions.title: Configure Stroke Caps and Miter Limits
stepByStepInstructions.instruction: Open the Stroke Studio (View > Studio > Stroke). Set Stroke width to 12 pt. Click 'Round Cap' to give the path friendly rounded ends. Under Join, select 'Miter Join' and set the Miter Limit to 1.4. Notice how acute corners automatically clip to a clean bevel if the angle is too sharp, preventing giant runaway spikes.

visualExamples.title: Cap Styles Comparison Matrix
visualExamples.description: How stroke endings behave in Affinity Designer.
visualExamples.visualContent:
| Cap Style | Terminal Geometry | Relationship to Endpoint Node |
|---|---|---|
| Butt Cap | Flat edge | Terminates exactly at the endpoint coordinate |
| Round Cap | Semicircular dome | Extends beyond endpoint by 1/2 stroke width |
| Square Cap | Flat rectangular box | Extends beyond endpoint by 1/2 stroke width |

visualExamples.title: Miter Limit Behavior Diagram
visualExamples.description: Why miter limits prevent needle spikes on sharp angles.
visualExamples.visualContent:
High Miter Limit (10.0): Acute Corner ===> Enormous sharp needle spike! (Breaks layout)
Balanced Miter (1.5-2.0): Acute Corner ===> Smoothly converts to neat bevel flat edge! (Safe)

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Runaway Miter Spikes protruding from acute corners
commonPitfalls.cause: Drawing a very acute sharp angle (e.g. 15 degrees) with a high Miter Limit (e.g. 10.0).
commonPitfalls.solution: Lower the Miter slider in the Stroke Studio to ~1.4 - 2.0, or switch Join style to 'Round Join' or 'Bevel Join'.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Join Curves button is disabled (grayed out)
commonPitfalls.cause: Both curves are already closed, or the selected nodes are intermediate nodes rather than open endpoints.
commonPitfalls.solution: Join Curves only operates on open end nodes of two curves. Use Break Curve first if you need to open a path.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Text-on-Path flowing upside down or backwards
commonPitfalls.cause: The curve was drawn from right to left; text always flows in the direction the curve was plotted.
commonPitfalls.solution: Select the curve with the Node Tool and click 'Reverse Curve' on the Context Toolbar.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the function of the 'Miter Limit' setting in the Stroke Studio?
options: It controls the transparency of the stroke.
It defines the maximum allowable ratio between miter length and stroke width before a sharp corner automatically converts into a bevel, preventing giant runaway spikes.
It sets the color of the path.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Miter Limit prevents ugly spikes at acute sharp corners by converting the point to a clean flat bevel whenever the spike exceeds the defined ratio threshold.

knowledgeCheck.question: What requirement must be met before two separate curves can be merged using the 'Join Curves' button?
options: Both curves must be grouped together.
Both curves must be selected, and their open endpoint nodes must be selected with the Node Tool.
The document must be in CMYK mode.
Both curves must have the exact same color fill.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Join Curves operates by welding the open terminal endpoints of two selected vector paths into a continuous single curve.

knowledgeCheck.question: If you attach text to a vector curve and the letters render upside down, which command instantly fixes the reading direction?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The 'Reverse Curve' action inverts the intrinsic mathematical winding direction of the path, flipping the orientation of Text-on-Path immediately.

summaryPoints: Open paths can be welded using Join Curves and split using Break Curve.
Closing curves forms airtight boundary perimeters ready for complex fills.
Cap styles (Butt, Round, Square) define how stroke terminals end.
Miter limits prevent needle spikes on sharp angles by cleanly transitioning to bevels.

slides.title: Path Operations, Joining, Breaking & Stroke Joins
slides.subtitle: Uniting Segments & Engineering Precision Stroke Terminals
slides.contentMarkdown:
Welcome to **Lesson D02-03**.

Real-world vector illustration frequently requires assembling complex graphics from multiple individual segments, splitting paths for color transitions, and fine-tuning stroke terminations.

In this lesson, you will master path topology: **Join, Break, Close, and Reverse**, alongside professional **Stroke Caps, Joins, and Miter Limits**.

actionBox.label: Mastery Goal
actionBox.text: Weld disparate curve fragments into a unified, mathematically clean closed shape.

slides.title: Path Topology: Open vs Closed Curves
slides.subtitle: Endpoints, Winding Order & Continuity
slides.contentMarkdown:
Vector curves possess directional and topological states:

1. **Open Curves:** Possess a distinct Start Node and End Node. Cap styles only apply to open curve ends.
2. **Closed Curves:** The start and end nodes are welded into a continuous perimeter loop with zero terminal ends.
3. **Path Direction (Winding):** Curves have an invisible chronological vector direction. Winding dictates which way Text-on-Path flows and how compound fills evaluate.

visual.content:
[Start Node ●] ════════════> Flow Direction ════════════> [End Node ●] (Open Curve)
                                  ↓ Close Curve
                      [ ● ═══════════════════ ● ]
                      [ ║                     ║ ] (Closed Perimeter Loop)
                      [ ● ═══════════════════ ● ]

slides.title: The Stroke Studio Architecture
slides.subtitle: Caps, Joins, Alignments & Miter Limits
slides.contentMarkdown:
Located in the right studio dock (`View > Studio > Stroke`), the Stroke panel controls physical stroke properties:

- **Cap Styles:**
  - *Butt Cap:* Terminates flat exactly on the anchor point.
  - *Round Cap:* Adds a smooth 180° rounded cap extending 1/2 stroke width.
  - *Square Cap:* Extends a flat rectangle 1/2 stroke width beyond the node.
- **Join Styles:**
  - *Miter Join:* Sharp pointed corners governed by the Miter Limit.
  - *Round Join:* Curvature corners.
  - *Bevel Join:* Chiseled flat corner bevels.

actionBox.label: Critical Control
actionBox.text: Keep Miter Limit around 1.4 to 2.0. Setting it too high generates runaway needle spikes on sharp angles!

slides.title: Step-by-Step: Welding Disconnected Curves
slides.subtitle: Executing the Join Curves Operation
slides.contentMarkdown:
Follow these steps to unite two separate vector paths into one:

1. **Step 1:** Select both curves using the Move Tool (`V`) or Node Tool (`A`) by holding `Shift`.
2. **Step 2:** Press `A` to switch to the Node Tool.
3. **Step 3:** Marquee-select the two open endpoints that you want to join.
4. **Step 4:** Look at the top Context Toolbar. Click the **'Join Curves'** icon.
5. **Inspect:** The two endpoints snap together into a single continuous vector path. Check the Layers Studio: the two layers have merged into one!

visual.content: Before: 2 Separate (Curve) Layers VS After: 1 Continuous Unified (Curve) Layer

slides.title: Reversing Path Direction for Text & Fills
slides.subtitle: Fixing Inverted Typography Flows
slides.contentMarkdown:
When you attach text to a path, it follows the chronological direction in which the path was plotted:

1. If text renders upside down along the bottom of an arc, select the curve with the Node Tool (`A`).
2. Click the **'Reverse Curve'** button on the Context Toolbar.
3. The starting node and ending node swap positions instantly, and the text immediately flips right-side up!

actionBox.label: Pro Tip
actionBox.text: Reverse Curve is essential when creating badges, circular logos, and currency seals.

slides.title: Path Traps & Common Failures
slides.subtitle: Avoid These Beginner Errors
slides.contentMarkdown:
### 1. The Needle Spike Disaster
- **The Issue:** A 2px corner produces a 200px long sharp needle spike protruding across the canvas.
- **The Cause:** Acute sharp angle with Miter Limit set to 10 or higher.
- **The Fix:** Lower Miter Limit to `1.5` or switch to `Round Join`.

### 2. Join Curves Grayed Out
- **The Cause:** The selected nodes are intermediate nodes along the body of the curve, not open terminal ends.
- **The Fix:** Join Curves requires open endpoints. Use `Break Curve` to split intermediate nodes first.

visual.content: Needle Spike (Miter > 5) | Safe Bevel (Miter 1.5) | Friendly Corner (Round Join)

slides.title: Independent Challenge: Precision Ribbon Seal
slides.subtitle: Put Path Operations into Action
slides.contentMarkdown:
### Your Mission:
Construct a multi-piece vector heraldic ribbon seal:

1. Draw 3 separate curve pieces: the front banner arc and two trailing ribbon tails.
2. Join and close the front banner into a solid closed curve filled with deep crimson `#990000`.
3. Configure stroke to `4 pt`, Miter Join with Miter Limit `2.0`.
4. Apply **Round Caps** to the tail flourishes and verify zero spikes.

### Acceptance Criteria:
- Front banner is 100% closed vector shape.
- Tail strokes have smooth rounded caps.
- Zero miter spikes protruding outside bounds.
